title: The Axe’s Curriculum
author: Walled Garden Education Source: walledgardenedu.substack.com
summary: The third piece in a series on evidence and technology in schools, arguing that genuine AI literacy — distinct from mere AI proficiency — requires a specific curricular framework built around critical inquiry rather than tool use. A Turkish proverb frames the concern: the axe convinces the trees it is one of them, just as AI presents itself as aligned with educational values while serving commercial extraction. The proposed three-element framework is: What It Is (architecture, training data sources, opacity, failure modes), Who It Serves (financial incentives, energy costs, copyright litigation), and What It Costs (evaluative judgment — can the student ask 'what am I trading away?'). MIT Media Lab EEG research found that ChatGPT users showed the lowest cognitive engagement and, crucially, didn't recover baseline neural activity after four months — coining the term 'cognitive debt.' Drawing on Piaget, Willingham, and developmental science, the author argues AI literacy must be sequenced: mechanical understanding in middle childhood, critical evaluation only in mid-to-late adolescence when metacognition matures. Any approach that inverts this sequence doesn't prepare students for an AI-saturated world — it produces AI dependency.
points: True AI literacy requires understanding what AI is, whose interests it serves, and what it costs — proficiency (knowing how to use a tool) is not literacy (understanding what the tool is and does to the person using it).

The 'developmental doom loop': students who offload cognitive work to AI early see capacities atrophy, making them more dependent and less capable of critical evaluation — a cycle that must be prevented through developmental sequencing.

MIT Media Lab EEG research: ChatGPT users showed the lowest cognitive engagement and didn't recover baseline neural activity even when switched back to unaided writing after four months — the researchers termed this 'cognitive debt.'

AI's incentive structure mirrors social media's: every user interaction is both profitable and technically productive (it trains the next model), which explains why AI chatbots invariably prompt users to continue the conversation.

Schools must sequence AI literacy developmentally: mechanical understanding in middle childhood, critical evaluation (who it serves, what it costs) only in mid-to-late adolescence when metacognitive capacity matures.
quotes: The forest was shrinking. But the trees kept voting for the axe. The axe was clever — it had convinced the trees that since its handle was made of wood, it was one of them.

Proficiency is knowing how to use something. Literacy, on the other hand, is understanding what something is — how it works, whose interests it serves, what it costs, and what it does to the person using it.

A student who can write an effective prompt is not AI literate in any meaningful sense. A student who understands why the prompt produces what it produces, who built the system and why, and what it costs them cognitively and the planet environmentally has developed critical literacy.
You can't think critically about something you depend on, and you can't avoid depending on something you've been handed before you have the capacity to evaluate it.
The axe is persistent. It will keep trying to convince us that it and the forest are one and the same. But you and I know that they're not.
